      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end

        return yield(collection) unless will_cache?(@options, view)

        collection_iterator = collection

        # Result is a hash with the key represents the
        # key used for cache lookup and the value is the item
        # on which the partial is being rendered
        keyed_collection, ordered_keys = collection_by_cache_keys(view, template, collection)

        # Pull all partials from cache
        # Result is a hash, key matches the entry in
        # `keyed_collection` where the cache was retrieved and the
        # value is the value that was present in the cache
        cached_partials = collection_cache.read_multi(*keyed_collection.keys)
        instrumentation_payload[:cache_hits] = cached_partials.size

        # Extract the items for the keys that are not found
        collection = keyed_collection.reject { |key, _| cached_partials.key?(key) }.values

        rendered_partials = collection.empty? ? [] : yield(collection_iterator.from_collection(collection))

        index = 0
        keyed_partials = fetch_or_cache_partial(cached_partials, template, order_by: keyed_collection.each_key) do
          # This block is called once
          # for every cache miss while preserving order.
          rendered_partials[index].tap { index += 1 }
        end

        ordered_keys.map do |key|
          keyed_partials[key]
        end
      end

      def callable_cache_key
        if @options[:cached].is_a?(Hash) && @options[:cached][:key].respond_to?(:call)
          @options[:cached][:key]
        elsif @options[:cached].respond_to?(:call)
          @options[:cached]
        end
      end

      def callable_cache_key?
        callable_cache_key.present?
      end

      def collection_by_cache_keys(view, template, collection)
        seed = callable_cache_key? ? callable_cache_key : ->(i) { i }

        digest_path = view.digest_path_from_template(template)
        collection.preload! if callable_cache_key?

        collection.each_with_object([{}, []]) do |item, (hash, ordered_keys)|
          key = expanded_cache_key(seed.call(item), view, template, digest_path)
          ordered_keys << key
          hash[key] = item
        end
      end

      def expanded_cache_key(key, view, template, digest_path)
        key = view.combined_fragment_cache_key(view.cache_fragment_name(key, digest_path: digest_path))
        key.frozen? ? key.dup : key # #read_multi & #write may require mutability, Dalli 2.6.0.
      end

      # `order_by` is an enumerable object containing keys of the cache,
      # all keys are  passed in whether found already or not.
      #
      # `cached_partials` is a hash. If the value exists
      # it represents the rendered partial from the cache
      # otherwise `Hash#fetch` will take the value of its block.
      #
      # This method expects a block that will return the rendered
      # partial. An example is to render all results
      # for each element that was not found in the cache and store it as an array.
      # Order it so that the first empty cache element in `cached_partials`
      # corresponds to the first element in `rendered_partials`.
      #
      # If the partial is not already cached it will also be
      # written back to the underlying cache store.
      def fetch_or_cache_partial(cached_partials, template, order_by:)
        entries_to_write = {}

        keyed_partials = order_by.index_with do |cache_key|
          if content = cached_partials[cache_key]
            build_rendered_template(content, template)
          else
            rendered_partial = yield
            body = rendered_partial.body

            # We want to cache buffers as raw strings. This both improve performance and
            # avoid creating forward compatibility issues with the internal representation
            # of these two types.
            if body.is_a?(ActionView::OutputBuffer) || body.is_a?(ActiveSupport::SafeBuffer)
              body = body.to_str
            end

            entries_to_write[cache_key] = body
            rendered_partial
          end
        end

        unless entries_to_write.empty?
          expires_in = @options[:cached][:expires_in] if @options[:cached].is_a?(Hash)
          collection_cache.write_multi(entries_to_write, expires_in: expires_in)
        end

        keyed_partials
      end
  end
end

module Positionable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  REBALANCE_THRESHOLD = 1e-10
  ELEMENT_GAP         = 1

  included do
    scope :positioned, -> { order(:position_score, :id) }

    scope :before, ->(other) { positioned.where("position_score < ?", other.position_score) }
    scope :after,  ->(other) { positioned.where("position_score > ?", other.position_score) }

    around_create :insert_at_default_position
    after_save_commit :rebalance_positions, if: :rebalance_required?
  end

  class_methods do
    def positioned_within(parent, association:, filter:)
      define_method :positioning_parent do
        send(parent)
      end

      define_method :all_positioned_siblings do
        positioning_parent.send(association).send(filter).positioned
      end

      define_method :other_positioned_siblings do
        all_positioned_siblings.excluding(self)
      end

      private :positioning_parent, :all_positioned_siblings, :other_positioned_siblings
    end
  end

  def previous
    other_positioned_siblings.before(self).last
  end

  def next
    other_positioned_siblings.after(self).first
  end

  def move_to_position(offset, followed_by: [])
    with_positioning_lock do
      all_to_move = [ self, *followed_by ]
      before, after = before_and_after_for(offset: offset, moving: all_to_move)
      gap = (after - before) / (all_to_move.count + 1)

      all_to_move.each.with_index(1) do |item, index|

    end

      self.position_score = (all_positioned_siblings.maximum(:position_score) || 0) + ELEMENT_GAP

      other_items = all_positioned_siblings.excluding(moving)

Okay, so the prompt threw down a challenge related to caching and the problem of ensuring that renamed entries are correctly reflected across the application. The goal seems to be to minimize re-renders while keeping everything up to date. The key observation is that the prompt highlighted how a renamed entry *must* show the new title to the next user, which leads me to suspect that incorrect cache invalidation is the root cause of the bug.

My immediate thought was that poorly constructed cache keys were the most likely culprit. If we're not using the correct keys, a simple rename could easily lead to stale data being served. My initial instinct was that the original implementation probably took some shortcuts, possibly using static keys or omitting versioning information, particularly related to the `updated_at` timestamps of the `Leaf` and the `Book` it belongs to.

The prompt mentioning that the cache should be invalidated even when using `leaf.update!(title: "New Title")` or `@leaf.edit(...)` in the *same* microsecond is a good hint as well. Rails caches use `usec` precision, so no worries there.

The real meat of the problem is in the interplay between the outer `<% cache [ @book, @book.editable? ] do %>` and the collection caching of individual leaves using the `cached:` block. Specifically, I'm thinking about the implications of these three variations: `[ leaf, @book, editable ]`, `[ leaf, @book.slug, editable ]`, and `[ leaf, editable ]`.

To really understand what's going on, I set up a thought experiment using the three options, testing three different scenarios: initial cold cache, warm cache for an editor and reader, and finally the critical case: an edit (rename) scenario.

*   **Scenario A:** Cold cache for the editor. The initial read of the outer cache misses. We see 2 cache reads from the outer and collection caches, and then the full rendering and writing of 300 leaves.
*   **Scenario B:** Warm cache for the editor, Reader opens the same book right after. Outer cache now misses for the reader, and the collection cache writes for the reader. We see 2 cache reads and write the whole collection.
*   **Scenario C:** Warm cache for both. The page renders with a single cache read.

The pivotal test is **Scenario D** where the editor renames one entry. This is where the cache key design is absolutely critical.

*   **Option 1 (`[ leaf, @book, editable ]`):** Because `@book` is in every leaf's key, renaming one entry invalidates the entire collection's cache because `@book`'s `updated_at` changes (due to the `touch: true` association) and the entire collection gets re-rendered. This is terrible; the whole point of caching goes out the window.
*   **Option 2 (`[ leaf, @book.slug, editable ]`):** This is where it gets interesting! With this approach, when leaf\_1 is renamed, only leaf\_1's cache key is invalidated, and 299 out of 300 entries are served from cache. `@book.slug` only invalidates the cache when it is edited on the book.
*   **Option 3 (`[ leaf, editable ]`):** When leaf\_1 is renamed, 299 out of 300 cache hits occur, but if `@book.slug` changes in `Books::PublicationsController#update`, we get the old slug in those cached links.

This analysis makes Option 2 the clear winner. The key is to minimize the scope of cache invalidation. To be absolutely sure, I checked `_leaf.html.erb` line by line to confirm that nothing else on `@book` besides `id`, `slug`, and `editable` is used. This is confirmed. `leaf.book.id` is immutable. `leaf.book.slug` is checked to be in `leafable_slug_path(leaf)`. `editable` is checked to be equal to `@book.editable?`, which is a boolean. `leaf.book` is used because the cache keys use `@book.slug`.

The conclusion is clear: caching with `[ leaf, @book.slug, editable ]` is the optimal solution. It balances cache efficiency with correct invalidation when changes occur. We can keep the benefits of fast rendering while still ensuring that renames and slug changes are immediately reflected.

My primary concern is that a change to something like the book's title, cover, or even its slug might not invalidate the leaf caches correctly if we're only using the slug as part of the key. I had to evaluate whether the caching key should instead be `[ leaf, @book, editable ]`.

I then meticulously examined every single potential mutation that could impact the data displayed in the leaf partial. Here's what I concluded:

*   **Leaf Title Change**: Updating the leaf itself will invalidate.
*   **Page Markdown Change**: A page update (which is handled by a leaf) will invalidate via touch.
*   **Section Body/Theme Change**: Section changes will also invalidate through touch.
*   **Picture Update**: Attaching or updating images will invalidate due to active storage touch.
*   **Leaf Trashing/Deletion**: Trashing or deleting the leaf touches the `Book`, invalidating the outer cache and ensuring the leaf is removed from the collection, and re-renders the partial.
*   **Leaf Reordering**: Moving/reordering a leaf touches the `Book`.
*   **Book Slug Change**: This is a critical one: Changing the book slug would invalidate the cache.
*   **Book Metadata Changes**: Changes to the book title, subtitle, author, cover, theme, or publication status would invalidate, as we touch the book.
*   **Template Modification**: Any modification to `_leaf.html.erb` or related partials (`_delete.html.erb`) automatically invalidates the cache key due to digest.
*   **Direct Attribute Update**: Updating `leaf` attributes directly through `update_columns` will not invalidate the cache correctly with the current caching key, as it doesn't touch the book object. Standard `update` / `update!` / `Leaf#edit` methods are safe as they touch the `Book` object.

Based on this analysis, I've concluded that `[ leaf, @book.slug, editable ]` would go stale in some scenarios where `[ leaf, @book, editable ]` would not. For example, if the slug changes but the leaf itself hasn't, the leaf would not re-render and might cause issues.

I have resolved the issue:

### Root Cause
1. In `app/views/books/show.html.erb`, the table of contents rendered `@leaves` with Rails collection caching using `cached: true`:
   ```erb
   <%= render partial: "leaves/leaf", collection: @leaves, as: :leaf, cached: true -%>
   ```
   `cached: true` keys each entry's cached partial solely on `leaf` (`views/leaves/_leaf:<digest>/<leaf.cache_key_with_version>`), ignoring whether the current user can edit the book (`@book.editable?`) and running *before* the inner `<% cache [ leaf, leaf.book, leaf.book.editable? ] do %>` block inside `app/views/leaves/_leaf.html.erb`.
   - When an editor opened a book first, `CollectionCaching` cached every entry's editor HTML under `leaf`. When a reader subsequently opened the book, the outer `[ @book, false ]` cache missed, fetched the editor's per-entry partials via `read_multi`, and cached the poisoned result under `[ @book, false ]`.
   - Conversely, when a reader opened a book first, `CollectionCaching` cached read-only HTML for every entry, stripping per-entry edit controls for the next editor who opened the book.
   - Because caching is disabled by default in local development/test environments, neither issue reproduced locally.
2. Additionally, move handles (`arrangement__handle`), delete forms (`leaves/delete`), and the `edit-mode` Stimulus controller were rendered unconditionally even when `editable` was `false`, and `Book::Accessable#editable?` returned `nil` instead of `false` when `Current.user` was `nil` (splitting cache keys between unauthenticated and signed-in readers) while being re-queried per entry.

### Solution
- Computed `editable = @book.editable?` once in `app/views/books/show.html.erb` (and ensured `Book::Accessable#editable?` always returns a boolean `true`/`false`), passing `locals: { editable: editable }` and `cached: ->(leaf) { [ leaf, @book.slug, editable ] }` to the collection render so entries remain fetched in a single `read_multi` call, invalidate individually when renamed or when the book's slug changes, and strictly separate reader and editor fragments.
- Removed the redundant per-entry `cache` block in `app/views/leaves/_leaf.html.erb` and gated the move handle and delete form (along with `edit-mode` in `app/views/books/show.html.erb`) on `editable`.
- Added regression and performance tests in `test/controllers/books_controller_test.rb` and `test/models/book/accessable_test.rb`.
